title: Security program: which initiatives do you fund, in what order, and how do you keep them on track?
short: Fund 8 to 12 initiatives on one 18-month roadmap, ranked by risk reduction per euro, and steer it monthly and quarterly.
answer: This quarter, turn the strategy's bets and your assessment gaps into 8 to 12 initiatives, each with an owner, an outcome, a one-time and a yearly cost and a target quarter, and have management approve the ranked roadmap with its budget. Then steer it in a monthly working group and a quarterly management review, and change scope, order or money only there.
audience: Heads of security, CISOs and IT leads who own security, and the managing directors who fund the program, especially in EU organizations with NIS2, BSIG or DORA duties

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Turn the gap list into a few initiatives.
items.text: Group the strategy's bets, maturity gaps, audit findings and risk register rows into 8 to 12 initiatives, each with one owner, an outcome and a date. Grundschutz++ asks you to link each measure to the requirements it meets and mark dependencies[^std3001].

items.title: Rank by risk reduction per euro.
items.text: Estimate which risks each initiative lowers and what it costs over three years. Digital providers under NIS2 must weigh the cost of implementation against the expected benefit[^nis2ir]. NIST describes funding from the top of the ranking until the money runs out[^ir8286b].

items.title: Schedule fixed deadlines first.
items.text: Put legal, audit and contract dates on the roadmap before ranking the rest, such as full CRA application on 11 December 2027 for product makers[^cra]. Then place prerequisites, like the asset inventory, before what depends on them.

items.title: Budget the run cost of every change.
items.text: Record one-time and recurring costs for each measure, as the BSI advises; it warns that savings on technical measures often turn into high ongoing staff effort[^std2002]. A tool without a named operator and a yearly budget won't protect anything.

items.title: Steer on a fixed cadence.
items.text: Track progress monthly and report to management at least quarterly, as the UK Cyber Governance Code expects of boards[^cgcop]. Change scope, order or budget only in those meetings, and minute each decision.

blocks.title: Build the roadmap in four weeks

items.title: Week 1: what goes in?
items.text: Collect the bets from the strategy sheet, the gaps from the maturity assessment, open audit and penetration test findings, risk register rows above appetite, incident lessons and every legal or contract deadline.

items.title: Week 2: which initiatives?
items.text: Merge measures that share a system or an owner. Grundschutz++ suggests weighing synergies between measures that meet several requirements at once[^std3001]. Write one line each: outcome, owner, one-time and yearly cost, dependencies.

items.title: Week 3: what makes the cut?
items.text: Score and rank them, draw the line at the budget and list what falls below it with the risk that stays. The BSI advises showing management that residual risk and letting it decide[^std2002].

items.title: Week 4: who approves?
items.text: Sequence by deadline, dependency and team capacity. Management approves the plan, since it has to provide the resources[^std3001]. The security projects sheet delivers each initiative from there.

blocks.title: Score each initiative on one line
items: **Risk reduction.** Which risk register rows it lowers, and by how much, in the register's own units: euros, hours of downtime or exposure bands. NIST advises stating the response cost in the same units as the risk[^ir8286b].
**Full cost.** One-time cost plus three years of licenses, staff time and support. NIST counts maintenance, installation, operating labor and disposal, not just the purchase[^ir8286b].
**Deadline.** A legal, audit, customer or insurer date overrides the ranking, but only for the part that date needs.
**Dependencies.** A prerequisite ranks with what it unblocks. The BSI's example: restrictive rights on a new server need a secure installation first[^std2002].
**Reach and speed.** Prefer broad effects and quick wins; the BSI notes these often come from organizational changes or central configuration settings[^std2002].
**Our rule.** Divide risk reduction by three-year cost, pull deadlines and prerequisites forward, then cut at the budget.

blocks.title: Budget size and structure
items: **Benchmark, don't target.** In ENISA's survey of 1,080 mostly large EU organizations, security took a median 9% of the IT budget and 10.6% of IT staff, the lowest staff share yet[^nisinv]. Sector medians ran from 6% in energy to 13.3% in ICT service management[^niscomp]. The security team sheet covers staffing.
**German firms report more.** In Bitkom's 2026 survey of companies with 10 or more staff, security took 18% of the IT budget on average, as in 2025; 45% spent 20% or more[^bitkom].
**Count like ENISA.** Include capital and operating spend on hardware, software, staff, contractors and outsourcing[^nisinv], or the comparison means nothing.
**Split run, change and reserve.** Run: staff, licenses, MDR and recurring tests and audits. Change: initiatives with an end date. Reserve: about 10% for incidents and findings.
**Under DORA, the board sets it.** The management body allocates and periodically reviews the budget for resilience, including training and ICT skills[^dora].

blocks.title: An 18-month roadmap, by half year
blocks.intro: An example for a mid-size company. Replace the initiatives with your own, but keep one owner and an outcome you can test for each.

columns.title: Months 1 to 6
items: **Admins on phishing-resistant sign-in.** Owner: head of IT. Done when every Tier 0 account uses a security key or passkey, as in the passkeys sheet.
**Timed ERP restore.** Owner: IT operations. Done when a restore test meets its recovery time objective.
**One asset and supplier list.** Owner: IT and procurement. Done when every entry has an owner; EDR coverage and supplier tiers depend on it.
**Overdue audit findings.** Owner: security. Done when each is closed with evidence.

columns.title: Months 7 to 12
items: **EDR on every server.** Owner: IT operations. Done when coverage is counted against the asset list and gaps are named.
**MDR with planted tests.** Owner: security. Done when a planted test is caught and escalated in the agreed time, as in the SOC and MDR sheet.
**Clauses for critical suppliers.** Owner: procurement. Done when top-tier contracts carry the third-party risk sheet's clauses.

columns.title: Months 13 to 18
items: **Management and backup zones.** Owner: network team. Done when admin interfaces answer only from the admin subnet.
**CRA readiness, if you make products.** Owner: product security. Done when vulnerability handling and SBOMs run before 11 December 2027[^cra].
**Reassess and replan.** Owner: head of security. Done when the maturity reassessment is in and the next roadmap is approved.

blocks.title: Get it funded
items: **Ask for outcomes, not products.** "Restore the ERP within 72 hours" survives a budget meeting; "a new backup appliance" invites a cheaper quote.

**Name the risk that stays if the answer is no.** NIS2 lets the cost of implementation count, but measures must still fit the risk[^nis2]. The BSIG weighs implementation costs the same way and requires documenting compliance[^bsig], so a no is a recorded management decision.

**Attach the outside demand.** Customer and supply chain requirements drove 26% and 29% of investment in ENISA's survey, board requests only 7%[^nisinv]. Add the customer clause, audit finding or insurer question to the request.

**Budget operators, not just tools.** ENISA sees money moving to technology and outsourcing rather than internal teams, and tools top the plans for new money at 47%[^nisinv]. Check what your current licenses include, and retire an overlapping tool for each one you add.

blocks.title: Steering cadence and the status page
items: **Monthly working group, 60 minutes.** Initiative owners, IT operations and security review status, blockers and dependencies, and decide small changes. Grundschutz++ asks for escalation paths for measures that slip, and for tracking by someone other than the implementer[^std3001].

**Quarterly management review.** Approve changes to scope, order and budget, and accept the risk of each delay. The BSI's model report covers risks, measure status, incidents, suppliers, audits, maturity, budget and open decisions[^bsicurr].
**Yearly replan before the budget.** Re-rank everything with the strategy review. Digital providers must review their risk treatment plan at least annually[^nis2ir].

**One status page.** A row per initiative: owner, outcome, due quarter, status in words and spend against plan. Below it: blockers and who must act, changes since last time, unplanned work and decisions needed. Outcome measures go on the security metrics sheet's board page.

blocks.title: Unplanned work and scope creep
items: **Plan 70 to 80% of capacity.** Keep the rest for incidents, audits and customer questionnaires, and log the hours so next year's reserve rests on data.

**One intake for new work.** Small requests go to the working group. Anything that moves a committed date goes to the quarterly review, and something else moves out. ENISA advises managing exceptions to the risk treatment plan explicitly[^enisatig].
**After an incident, replan.** Digital providers must feed post-incident reviews into their risk treatment[^nis2ir]. Re-rank at the next monthly meeting, not in the crisis.
**Give audit findings an owner and a date.** The BSI can require critical facility operators to submit a plan to fix deficiencies their audits found[^bsig].
**Split off phase two.** When an initiative grows, close the agreed scope and let the rest compete for funding.

blocks.title: Close initiatives with evidence
items: **Done means the outcome was tested.** Not "tool installed" but "the restore ran in time". The security projects sheet covers the definition of done.

**File the evidence.** Grundschutz++ asks you to record for each measure the requirement, the date it was implemented or checked and who documented or checked it, with the evidence attached[^std3001].
**Hand over to run.** Name the operating owner, move the yearly cost into the run budget and add a measure to the metric set.
**Re-rate the risks.** Update the register rows the initiative was meant to lower. The BSI expects the security officer to report progress and the resulting risk reduction to management[^std2002].
**Compare plan with actuals.** Record cost and time against the estimate to correct the next ranking.

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **Portfolio management software.** For 8 to 12 initiatives a spreadsheet or the ticket system is enough; Grundschutz++ names a project or ticket system for owners and deadlines[^std3001].
**Detailed plans beyond two quarters.** Plan the next six months by task, the rest by half year.
**Exact ROI for every initiative.** Quantify only the close calls; see the risk register sheet.
**Percent complete.** Report outcomes reached and dates held.
**One program per law.** Run one roadmap and tag each initiative with the NIS2, DORA, CRA or ISO 27001 requirement it serves.

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Funding the project, not its operation.** The tool goes live and nobody has hours to tune it.
**Starting everything at once.** Cap the initiatives in flight at what your owners can run, and finish before starting.
**Green until the last month.** Ask for the next milestone and its date, not a color.
**Reprioritizing in the corridor.** Each incident or executive request reshuffles the plan unless changes go through the review.
**Counting go-live as done.** Whether people use it decides whether the risk dropped; the security projects sheet covers measuring adoption.

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **ENISA's latest data shows the shift to tools.** Its December 2025 report found security spend steady at a median 9% of IT budgets but moving to technology and outsourcing, while security staff fell to 10.6% of IT staff[^nisinv]. Budget the people who run each new tool.

**Grundschutz++ describes a managed implementation plan.** BSI-Standard 300-1 (October 2026) prioritizes measures by effort, synergies, risk, strategic value and quick wins, sets owners and deadlines, tracks progress with escalation and reports the risk of open items to management[^std3001].

**German critical facilities got physical resilience duties.** The KRITIS umbrella act took effect on 17 March 2026. Its risk assessment duty applies 9 months after a facility's registration, resilience measures, incident reporting and the management duty 10 months after[^kritis]. Plan them on the same roadmap.

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: Keep one page of 3 to 5 initiatives with your IT provider and review it quarterly with the managing director.
Ask the provider to price each one-time and monthly, and add the monthly part to the service contract.
Fund a tested restore and phishing-resistant admin sign-in before any new tool.

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Run 8 to 12 initiatives with a monthly working group and a quarterly management review.
Keep the roadmap and status page in a spreadsheet or the ticket system, linked to risk register rows.
Hold back 20 to 30% of team capacity for incidents, audits and questionnaires.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: Run one group roadmap with a view per legal entity; each regulated entity's management approves its part.
Under DORA, minute the management body's yearly budget allocation and review[^dora].
Have internal audit sample closed initiatives for evidence every year.

changes.text: First draft, based on ENISA's NIS Investments 2025 and NIS2 implementation guidance, Bitkom's Wirtschaftsschutz 2026 survey, BSI-Standards 200-2 and 300-1, the BSI's 2026 management training curriculum, NIST IR 8286B, NIS2, Regulation 2024/2690, DORA, the CRA, the BSIG, the KRITIS umbrella act and the UK Cyber Governance Code.
